claim: A frequency byte does not drive a formula and does not have a hundred and twenty-eight values. Its top four bits index a table of sixteen entries, so eight settings share each entry, and the entries are the named third octaves between the two frequencies the page prints against that address -- with one that is not. On 200 - 6.3k, fifteen of the sixteen sit within 0.07 octaves of 200, 250, 400, 500, 630, 800, 1k, 1.25k, 1.6k, 2k, 2.5k, 3.15k, 4k, 5k and 6.3k, a median 0.03 and under what a twelfth-octave reading resolves. The third entry sits at 279 Hz where the series says 315, which is 0.18 octaves and two bands, and it is the only entry the reading and the series disagree about. Both mid sections return that same 279, and they return the whole of the first four entries to within 0.002 octaves of each other, so the two index one table rather than two. Read across its own eight settings the entry does not move -- 279.1, 278.7, 278.8 and 279.0 at 16, 17, 20 and 23 -- and the settings either side of it return the entries either side, so the stride is eight and the number in the table is 279.
named: a third-octave coefficient table indexed by the byte's high nibble, with one entry that is not a third octave
adds: Each record says which band the deviation was largest in at each setting it was asked at, where a curve fitted over the whole feature puts its top, and says in as many words that no filter, no corner and no order is in it. Nothing in any of them says the readings are entries of a table, that the table has sixteen of them, that eight settings share one, that the two mid sections share it, or that the entries are the third octaves the page's two ends bracket. That is the whole of what is added here, and it is added by holding five candidate laws against the same readings rather than by fitting one to them.
refutedBy: Two settings inside one of these entries returning frequencies the run tells apart, or two settings across an entry boundary returning frequencies it does not. Either is measurable at settings 4 through 12 of any slot printed with a frequency range. Or a slot on the same printed range whose readings do not land on this series at all, which would make the table a property of the type rather than of the range.

eraPriors.claim: A frequency parameter of this period is a table of filter coefficients indexed by the byte, not a frequency the part computes coefficients from.
eraPriors.why: Turning a frequency into a biquad needs a sine and a tangent, which a small control processor of the era would run once per parameter change and would rather not. Storing the coefficients instead makes the entry expensive in memory, which is why the table is short where a rate table is not: a rate entry is one number and a filter entry is a set.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: Two settings inside one entry returned different frequencies at a resolution the run can tell apart, or the number of distinct values across the byte turned out to be near a hundred and twenty-eight.

eraPriors.claim: A table's stride is a power of two, because dividing by one is a shift.
eraPriors.why: A hundred and twenty-eight settings over sixteen entries is eight each. A table of twenty entries would need a divide or a second table, which is the reason the printed range that holds twenty third octaves is expected to behave differently and is the run this claim queues.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The entry boundaries turned out not to fall on multiples of eight -- which is measurable at settings 6, 7, 8 and 9 and has not been asked.

community.claim: Read out of the program of Roland's own later software rendering of this line: a frequency parameter there carries no frequency but selects one of a short list of stored coefficient sets; a shelf's corner is a choice between two such lists rather than a setting that varies; a gain indexes a short table and a byte past its ends is ignored rather than clamped; and the list a frequency selects from is sixteen entries once the one slot that resolves to the selection's own fallback is counted out. What was read is a rendering written years after the hardware, carrying the material of three earlier units of this line and not of this one, so none of it is evidence about what this unit's table holds -- it is a second design of the same decade by the same maker, which is what the era prior above is made of and no more. It leans where the second alternative leans and settles nothing: that a parameter is a table in one design is silent on where another design's entries sit, and the run that would separate the two is the one already queued under what this does not close. It was read after this claim was made and after the records it rests on were published.
community.source: The TabulaSonora project's reverse-engineering record of the Roland SOUND Canvas VA voice: docs/FINDINGS.md in its spec repository, and the insertion-effect source of its NativeTS engine. Read 2026-09-13.

alternatives.reading: The entries are sixteen frequencies at equal ratios between the printed ends rather than the named third octaves. On a range whose ends bracket sixteen third octaves the two are the same series to within a third of a percent, and both ranges this claim has been read on are such a range.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: Measured on 100 - 8.0k, the one printed range on this unit whose ends bracket a number of third octaves that is not sixteen. Read as the corner of the all-pass ladder the byte moves, at every eighth value and at the three pairs that straddle a stride of eight, the byte turns out to have no sixteen entry table on it: 7 to 8 moves 0.056 octaves, 15 to 16 moves 0.037 and 63 to 64 moves 0.059, against 0.307 between 8 and 15 and 0.478 between 56 and 63 -- which are pairs inside what would be a single entry. Neither series survives it either: scaled onto the sixteen settings on the grid, the named third octaves need a factor that drifts 1.55 octaves and equal ratios one that drifts 2.69. The corner is read to 0.030 octaves, so both are out by more than fifty times the reading. See inferences/roland-sc8850-01/0120-eight-allpass-sections-summed-with-the-dry.json.

alternatives.reading: The three entries are 200, 250 and 315 and the filter built from them does not peak there. A table entry of this period is a set of coefficients rather than a frequency, so what is stored is already the filter -- and a section whose response below 300 Hz is not the peaking biquad the model renders would put its top somewhere else while the entry behind it is exactly the named one.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The run it asked for was made and it split the three. Sweeping the width byte with the frequency byte at the bottom moved the top 0.149 octaves, against 0.024 for the same sweep at the middle of the range -- six times the control where the margin asked for 1.8 -- and at the two narrowest widths the top landed on 198.8 and 198.6 Hz, which is the printed 200 to a hundredth of an octave. So the first entry is 200 and the filter built from it does peak there; what did not was the shape it was read through. Read again at the narrowest width the second entry moved inside the floor, from 240.3 to 240.5 against a printed 250, which is 0.056 octaves and less than one band. The third did not move at all: 279.7 at width 2, 280.1 at width 3, 279.1 at width 4. Two of the three were the width and the third is the table.

separatedBy.divergence: 0.15 octaves, which is how far below the named series the three low entries read and is what either answer has to account for

predicts.the entry is where it is read: The fitted position holds within a few hundredths of an octave across the width byte's values, exactly as it does at setting 64, and stays near 179 Hz at all of them.
predicts.the section is not a biquad down there: The fitted position moves with the width byte by more than the band it is read against, because a response that is not symmetric in log frequency is read at a different place as its flanks change.

run.why_this_shape: The same sweep the width byte already has at data/units/roland-sc8850-01/efx-bands/01-00-08-where-the-eq-hinges-in-twelfths.json, with the frequency byte at 0 instead of 64. That record is the control this one is read against, so it is the one run that answers the question and nothing else has to be repeated. Only six settings because the byte answers to 0 through 4 and reads everything above as 0, which that record already showed.

alternatives.reading: The three entries below 315 Hz really are 200, 250 and 315 and the disagreement is the reading, not the table: the largest band of a peak this wide is a coarse estimator, and the peak's top is flat enough that a tenth of a decibel moves it.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The reading it asked for was made and says the opposite. Located by a fit over the whole feature rather than by the largest band, the three entries read 179.2, 240.3 and 279.7 Hz against 200, 250 and 315 -- 0.06 to 0.17 octaves low, where the same reading puts every entry above them inside a fifth of a band of the model. It is not scatter in the fit: the other mid section, which shares nothing with this one but the table, reads 179.1 Hz at the same setting, and the same takes read at a third of an octave instead of a twelfth put the low group 0.13 octaves out rather than 0.15. It is not the feature's width being read as its place either: the width byte of this section moves the fitted position by 0.024 octaves across every value it answers to, while moving the window that position is fitted over from four bands to forty-nine.

alternatives.reading: Thirty-two entries at equal ratios, four settings each.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It puts settings 0 and 4 in different entries and settings 8 and 12 in different entries. The reading tells neither pair apart, and the pairs are the settings the run asked precisely because four apart is where a finer table would show.

alternatives.reading: Eight entries at equal ratios, sixteen settings each.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It puts settings 0 and 8 in one entry. The reading tells them apart by five bands.

alternatives.reading: No table: the printed ends of a ratio scale over all 128 settings.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It gives every setting its own frequency, so settings 0 and 4 and settings 8 and 12 are all distinct. The reading tells neither pair apart. It is also two bands out at seven of the twelve settings, where the winner is exact.

alternatives.reading: No table: the printed ends of an evenly divided line in hertz.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It is 1.75 octaves out in the middle of the byte, which is twenty-one bands.

alternatives.reading: The table is the type's rather than the printed range's. Both types this has been read on put a filter section in front of something and both were read on a range the page prints against a filter's own corner -- an equaliser's mid and a chorus's pre-filter. What picks the entries could be the type rather than the ends the page prints, and every slot that would tell them apart is unmeasured.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The run it asked for was made and the prediction held at every setting. Ten entries of a third printed range, on a type that shares no stage with either of the two already read, land on the third octaves that range's printed ends bracket to a median 0.0053 octaves and a worst 0.0179, where one band of the reading is 0.0847. A table belonging to the type would have to hold the entries of a range it has no reason to know about.

separatedBy.observable: Where the entries of 315 - 8k/Bypass fall, read on a delay's damping against the same chain with the last position selected.

predicts.the printed range chooses the table: The third octaves this range brackets and no others: 315, 400, 500, 630, 800, 1250, 2000, 3150, 5000 and 8000 at the ten settings asked, reached by the byte's high nibble the way the two ranges already read are reached. Fourteen third octaves fit between these printed ends where fifteen fit between the other two's, and the page prints the position left over as the filter out -- so the table has sixteen slots on every range and the page says what fills them.
predicts.the table is the type's: Entries that are not this range's third octaves -- either the series one of the ranges already read holds, which would make the table the same table wherever it is reached from, or something neither of them holds, which would make it the type's.

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: One twelfth-octave band, 0.083 octaves, which is the resolution the two readings behind this claim were made at. One entry of the table is a third octave, 0.333, and the two candidate answers differ by at least one entry at every setting asked.

run.why_this_slot: A delay with its feedback parked at the centre of -98% - +98%, which is none, returns one copy of the note and the damping is the only thing shaping it. That the damping acts at all with the loop open was asked before this was queued rather than assumed, because a damping control sitting in the feedback loop would come back flat under this parking and read exactly like a byte that does nothing. It acts: two settings one entry apart move the top of the band set by 2.1 dB, and 20 log10(400 / 315) is 2.07, which also says the filter is first order and that the byte is reached by its high nibble -- setting 15 is the second entry and not the sixteenth position.
run.why_the_reference_is_a_setting: The last position of this printed range is the filter out, so the null a corner is read against is one value of the byte being swept rather than another byte switched. The unit's own reset leaves it there.

alternatives.reading: The 279.1 Hz belongs to the series every printed range is cut from, so the same element read on any range returns it.

residual.why: Zero at every entry but one under the band reading: the model's rendered profile peaks in the unit's own band at fifteen of the sixteen. The one it misses is the third, by two bands. what_moved_the_verdict.why: Two records that sweep the byte inside its third entry alone were added to the set. The model puts that entry where the printed series does and the unit does not, so the residual is the same 0.167 octaves at every setting of them -- and a record that deliberately moves the byte inside one entry has almost no span of its own for that to be a share of. On 01-00-07-the-entry-that-is-not-printed-in-twelfths.json the span is 0.250 octaves and the median residual is 0.1668, which is 0.668 of it against a ceiling of 0.2. what_moved_the_verdict.what_is_new_in_it: Nothing about the unit. The entry that misses is the same entry, by the same 0.167 octaves, and no reading of any byte changed. What changed is that the archive now holds a record whose whole span is inside that entry, so the one departure this class has is being asked to be a small share of a small number.

extra.key: a note on what it replaces
extra.text: That claim's sentence already says a centre moves for every eighth value of its byte, and its model does not: the model carries the twelve settings the run asked and interpolates between them, which is the measurement wearing the clothes of a law. This is the same sentence held against a catalogue instead of asserted, and with the entries named. Nothing about the chain around it changes -- the model here is that model with one map swapped, so that the residual answers one question.

extra.key: a note on what was left out
extra.text: The first pass over this class scored the same five candidates as whole band profiles in decibels and returned `equivalent_under_this_test`: every candidate passed the gross gate and none leaned. That was not the candidates agreeing. Sliding a peak of this width by a sixth of an octave costs a decibel or two on its flanks and nothing at its top, so the residual in decibels stayed under the run's own floor for candidates that were two bands out at every setting -- and a residual that is the same size everywhere does not lean, so the gate that catches a wrong structure could not catch a wrong place either. The reading was changed, not the gate's threshold: where the feature sits is what the byte moves, and the record already published it. The reading it was changed to was then changed again, and this is the second half of the same lesson. The largest band is quantised to a band, so a peak halfway between two of them cannot be read closer than half a band however good the takes are, and on a broad feature a tenth of a decibel decides which of the two it is: the width byte above moves it two bands without moving the feature at all. A fit over the whole feature is not quantised and does not do that -- and it has a bias the largest band does not, because a symmetric curve fitted to a feature whose flanks are not symmetric tops out towards the longer one. Neither reading is the better one, which is why the record now publishes both, and why what was done here was to score the same candidates twice rather than to swap one reading for the other. The finding is what survived both.

This claim is read on bytes that set a filter corner and leave it there, and it does not extend to every byte a page prints a frequency range against. The one such byte measured outside that description -- the centre a phaser's modulator sweeps, on 100 - 8.0k -- moves at every setting and has no sixteen entry table on it. Which is what a byte that has to be swept smoothly would have to do: sixteen entries under a modulator is sixteen audible steps. So the sixteen entries belong to a stored coefficient set that is chosen once, and the two kinds of frequency byte are not one class.
